chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Abī Yaḥyā al-Wāsiṭī, from some of our companions, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام was brought a grave-robber, so he delayed his punishment until Friday. Then when Friday came, he cast him beneath the feet of the people, and they continued trampling him with their feet until he died.

So these narrations are to be understood as meaning that when the act is repeated by them three times, and the hadd has been carried out upon them, then at that point killing becomes obligatory upon them just as it becomes obligatory upon the thief; and the Imam has the choice regarding the manner of killing, however he wishes, according to what he sees to be more deterrent in the immediate circumstance.

key_terms.أَرْدَعَ: more deterrent, more effective in restraining others
key_terms.السَّارِقِ: the thief, used here as a legal analogy
key_terms.الْإِمَامُ: the Imam, the lawful authority who determines implementation
key_terms.نَبَّاشٍ: a grave-robber, one who exhumes graves unlawfully

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Shia hadith on a grave-robber who repeatedly commits the offense after the hadd has been enforced?
ai.summary: This report describes the punishment of a grave-robber before Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام and then explains the juristic understanding of such narrations. It states that if the offense is repeated three times and the hadd has already been enforced, then execution becomes obligatory, with the Imam authorized to choose the manner that is most deterrent.
